summary: An excerpt from Michael Mann's "Our Fragile Moment" describes the Permian-Triassic extinction (the Great Dying), about 250 million years ago, driven partly by a massive carbon release that caused extreme warming, drying and a drop in atmospheric oxygen. The oxygen crash doomed the dominant synapsids and therapsids, including the "beast tooth" Theriodontia, while diapsids such as archosaurs, with more efficient respiration, thrived and set the stage for dinosaurs. Only a few proto-mammals, such as Cynodontia, survived. Mann asks whether this event is an analog for a human-caused sixth mass extinction.
one_line: Michael Mann explains how CO2-driven warming and falling oxygen in the Great Dying wiped out Permian proto-mammals and let early dinosaurs rise.
key_facts: The Great Dying, or Permian-Triassic (P-T) extinction, occurred roughly 250 million years ago and appears to have resulted at least partly from a massive heat-inducing release of carbon into the atmosphere.
An estimated 90% of all Permian species disappeared in the P-T extinction, and 96% of marine species perished.

Trilobites, distant ancestors of the modern horseshoe crab, were wiped out after a nearly 300-million-year run; the giant dragonfly Meganeuropsis, with a nearly three-foot (0.9 meter) wingspan, also vanished.
On land, more than two thirds of amphibian and reptile species and nearly one third of insect species were wiped out.

The Ordovician glaciation around 450 million years ago, on the South Pole–centered supercontinent Gondwana, killed about half of all existing genuses and was the first widely recognized mass extinction.
The Cambrian explosion saw most of today's life emerge in the first 10 million years of the period, aided by rising oxygen and the stratospheric ozone layer.
Paleozoic oxygen concentrations climbed as high as 35%, versus 21% today, favoring synapsids, which had high metabolisms and a single hole on each side of the skull.
Theriodontia (Latin for "beast tooth") were therapsids with wider-opening jaws, larger skulls, specialized teeth and more powerful jaws, and seemed primed to take over.
At the P-T boundary, CO2 spiked, and the supercontinent Pangea became hotter and drier, killing forests and cutting organic matter burial.
Atmospheric oxygen dropped as low as 15% at the P-T boundary, producing widespread hypoxia that hurt synapsids and therapsids.
Diapsids, which have two holes on each side of the skull, include reptiles, birds and dinosaurs; archosaurs used a more efficient respiratory system to gain an edge when oxygen plummeted.
Cynodontia ("dog teeth"), ancestors of all mammals, survived, growing up to six feet (1.8 m) long at first but shrinking to the size of field mice by the end of the Triassic.
